title: Better engines for ai game dev? What about specific libraries for things like rendering, etc?
author: Legal_Suggestion4873
selftext:
I'm an Unreal Engine user, but I make a lot of custom stuff in it (always have, even before AI).

Right now, the biggest draw for it is rendering (nanite + lumen is nice), the built in materials, niagara, etc., but more and more working with it is becoming so burdensome compared to the rest of the gameplay logic. 

I'm pretty sure a fully code based engine is just going to make the most sense now. If there is any editor at all, it'll be something that can be used for humans to make modifications to files, but it shouldn't be \*the\* way, if that makes sense. 

So I'm looking for engines that are useful for this. I know of Bevy, Kaiju, etc., but I'm looking for more. I've been debating if it makes sense to just make an engine by strapping together various libraries. I'm not much of an *engineer*, more like a 'technical gameplay designer' if that makes sense. I don't know a lot about the rendering pipeline - its pretty untouchable in UE - but I feel like that's really the only issue I have. I know a lot about everything else. 

Anyone have any resources or suggestions?

comments.author: SeasawPhilosopher
comments.body:
I’m working on an Arena FPS and have been using browser/threejs for the time being but eventually want a native version. I tested porting to both Unreal 5.8 and Godot and it was kinda painful. The unreal port took forever and didn’t preserve the mechanics fully or the graphics, and then working with Unreal via AI was a total pain in the ass. Godot was better but still painful compared to the web workflow.

I realized that engines are way too opaque to codex, and it works so well with the browser stack becuse it can just modify code and assets directly and run and valid easily. Even with MCP modern engines seem to really slow AI down, and I don’t see a way around that unless an engine is built from the ground up to work well with AI.

I started thinking like you that a pure code solution is the way to go. Single language, don’t even bother with a scripting language. So I had codex port my game but this time make an a la carte modern c++ engine from existing libraries like SDL3, bgfx, imgui, and fill in what’s missing itself. The port was completed much faster than the unreal or godot ports and the game was replicated perfectly. I did throw the port away and for now I’m still working on the browser stack, but I think this is the route I’ll end up going.

replies.author: Legal_Suggestion4873
replies.body:
Thats interesting, and exactly what I'm thinking too. 

No need for all these layers of nonsense. Nobody touches code anymore anyway.

I've been using AI to make frameworks in Unreal Engine, and it's working great, but the more i think about it, the more I'm wondering what is even the point?

Do I even need a reusable framework? If anything I just need a clean spec about the framework, let it do it again later when the whatever-generation is out and can do it even easier
